title: Investment Sizing & Comparable Valuation
description: Master advanced techniques for sizing investments, triangulating valuations with comparables, and stress-testing deal logic under uncertainty.

interactions.prompt: A SaaS company has $80M ARR growing 40% YoY with 75% gross margins. Using the 'Rule of 40' premium framework, what's a reasonable EV/Revenue multiple?

options.text: ~8x — moderate growth doesn't justify premium
~15x — Rule of 40 score of 115 commands top-decile multiple
~25x — growth rate alone drives the multiple
~4x — gross margins are irrelevant to revenue multiples

interactions.teachingPreamble: The 'Rule of 40' says revenue growth rate + profit margin should exceed 40% for healthy SaaS. Companies scoring well above 40 (like growth + margin = 115) historically trade at 15-20x revenue. But the real power is using this as a guesstimation anchor: score above 40 → premium multiple; below → discount.

interactions.prompt: Datadog trades at 18x EV/Revenue, CrowdStrike at 20x, and Snowflake at 30x. All grow 35-50% YoY. A private cybersecurity startup growing 45% YoY seeks a $2B valuation on $100M ARR. What's the key signal?

options.text: 20x is fair — matches CrowdStrike's public comparable directly
Apply a 25-35% illiquidity discount to public comps, targeting ~13-15x
Use Snowflake's 30x since growth rates are similar
Public comps are irrelevant for private valuations

interactions.prompt: You're sizing a Series B investment in a fintech with $15M ARR. The fund targets 3x gross return in 5 years. If you assume a 15x exit multiple and 30% dilution from future rounds, what should today's post-money valuation cap be?

options.text: ~$225M — just multiply ARR by 15x
~$53M — back-solve from exit, accounting for dilution and return target
~$150M — exit value divided by 3x return target
~$105M — exit value divided by return, adjusted for dilution

interactions.teachingPreamble: Sophisticated investors back-solve entry valuations from target returns. If a company will be worth $X at exit, you divide by your target return multiple, then adjust for dilution from future funding rounds. This 'venture math' framework: Exit Value ÷ Return Target × (1 - Dilution) = Max Entry Valuation. Here: exit ~$450M (assuming ARR triples to $45M × 15x), ÷ 3x = $150M, × 0.70 for dilution = ~$105M.

interactions.prompt: In a leveraged buyout, if you acquire a company at 8x EBITDA with 60% debt and the exit multiple remains 8x, the primary driver of equity returns is ____ rather than multiple expansion.

options.text: Revenue growth from new market entry
Debt paydown from free cash flow generation
Reducing the cost of capital via refinancing
Increasing the dividend payout ratio over time

interactions.prompt: You can invest $50M at a $200M pre-money in Company A (marketplace, 80% take rate, 3x YoY growth, -40% margins) or Company B (B2B SaaS, 90% gross margins, 60% YoY growth, +10% margins). Same TAM estimate of $15B. Which do you choose and why?

options.text: Company A — hypergrowth marketplaces with high take rates dominate winner-take-all markets
Company B — profitable growth de-risks the investment and signals capital efficiency
Company A — but negotiate a 1.5x liquidation preference to hedge burn risk
Company B — but only with a ratchet clause tied to growth maintaining 50%+

interactions.prompt: A PE firm evaluates acquiring a $500M revenue industrial company. Public comps trade at 12x EV/EBITDA, precedent transactions closed at 15x, and a DCF (10% WACC, 2% terminal growth) yields 13x implied. What's the best estimate for a fair offer?

options.text: 12x — always anchor to where public markets trade today
15x — precedent transactions reflect real control premiums paid
13-14x — triangulate methods, weighting DCF and precedents over trading comps
10x — apply a discount for current macro uncertainty

interactions.teachingPreamble: Professional valuations triangulate across three methods: trading comparables (public market mood), precedent transactions (what acquirers actually paid, including control premiums), and DCF (intrinsic value). The key guesstimation insight: precedent transactions typically run 20-40% above trading comps due to control premiums and synergies. A weighted blend — heavier on DCF and precedents for M&A — gives the most defensible range.

interactions.prompt: You're estimating the valuation of a pre-revenue biotech with a Phase 2 drug candidate. Rank these valuation approaches from most to least appropriate for this specific situation.

options.text: EV/Revenue multiples from comparable public biotechs
Risk-adjusted NPV of expected drug cash flows by phase probability
Sum-of-parts using comparable licensing deal values per indication
Standard DCF with 5-year revenue projections and terminal value

interactions.prompt: Interest rates just spiked 200bps. Your target's DCF used a 10% WACC. The PE fund's LBO model assumed 5% senior debt. How does your bid strategy change?

options.text: Lower bid 15-20% — higher WACC crushes DCF and debt costs erode LBO returns
Maintain bid but restructure with more equity and less leverage
Walk away — rate spikes make all acquisitions uninvestable
Increase bid to lock in the deal before rates rise further

interactions.priorContext: Previously you triangulated a 13-14x EBITDA offer using a 10% WACC DCF, 12x trading comps, and 15x precedent transactions. Now rates have spiked 200bps, raising your WACC to ~12% and senior debt costs to ~7%, fundamentally changing both intrinsic value and leveraged return math.
